Q7283727.title: Raid on Scone
paras: In 1296 Edward I of England deposed King John Balliol and ruled Scotland through his own officials. One of them was William de Ormesby, an English judge made Justice of Scotland when Earl Warenne became warden of the conquered kingdom. Edward ordered him to take oaths of homage and fealty from Scotland's landholders, and Ormesby did so with notorious severity, driving those who refused into exile.

In the spring of 1297 the Scots rose against English rule in several places at once. After killing the English sheriff of Lanark in May, William Wallace joined forces with Sir William Douglas, 'the Hardy', and the two led a raid on Scone, the old royal centre near Perth where Ormesby then was. Ormesby was warned at the last moment and escaped with great difficulty, but he had to leave all his property behind as spoil for the raiders. The Scots took control of Scone.

The raid was both practical and symbolic: it drove the chief English law officer out of the heart of the kingdom and struck at the place where Scottish kings had been inaugurated. Sources differ on the month: the Wikipedia article on the raid dates it to June 1297, while the Dictionary of National Biography and the Wikipedia article on Ormesby place it at the outbreak of Wallace's revolt in May.

Douglas was soon captured by the English after the Scottish nobles' capitulation at Irvine, but Wallace kept fighting. Joining Andrew Moray, who had raised the north, he won the Battle of Stirling Bridge on 11 September 1297 and became Guardian of Scotland. Ormesby survived to serve Edward I in England, raising foot soldiers in October 1297 after the defeat at Stirling.

Q83224.title: Battle of Hastings
Q83224.place: Near Hastings, Sussex (today Battle, East Sussex)
paras: The battle was fought on 14 October 1066 between the English army of King Harold Godwinson and the invading army of William, Duke of Normandy, with commanders such as William fitzOsbern and Eustace II of Boulogne. Modern estimates put each army at somewhere between about 5,000 and 13,000 men; contemporary Norman figures are wildly exaggerated.

It was a war of succession. Edward the Confessor died childless on 5 January 1066 and Harold was crowned, but Duke William claimed that Edward had promised him the throne, and King Harald Hardrada of Norway also claimed it. Hardrada invaded the north with Harold's exiled brother Tostig; Harold destroyed their army at Stamford Bridge on 25 September. Three days later, on 28 September, William landed at Pevensey on the south coast and fortified Hastings, forcing Harold to march south again.

Fighting began in the morning and lasted until dusk. The English stood in a shield wall along a ridge; Norman archers shooting uphill and attacks by infantry and mounted knights failed to break it. When part of William's army fell back and a rumour spread that he was dead, William rode among his men to show himself and turned the retreat into a counter-attack against the English who had pursued them. Norman chroniclers say the Normans then used feigned flights to draw more men out of the line; most historians accept this, though some think it a later embellishment. Late in the day Harold was killed, and his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine also died.

How Harold died is uncertain. The famous arrow in the eye rests on a later tradition and an ambiguous scene of the Bayeux Tapestry, which was restored in the 19th century; the earliest written mention of the arrow dates from the 1080s, and other accounts say he was cut down by knights.

The victory did not end English resistance at once, but after William marched on London the English leaders submitted to him at Berkhamsted, and he was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066. Rebellions continued for years, answered by the Harrying of the North in 1069-1070. William founded Battle Abbey on the site.

Q12519.title: Magna Carta
Q12519.place: Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines (Kingdom of England)
paras: Magna Carta was the peace settlement between King John of England and a party of rebel barons. Its text is dated 15 June 1215 at the meadow of Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines; talks had begun there on 10 June, and on 19 June John announced to his officials that peace had been restored. Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, mediated and helped turn the barons' written demands, the 'Articles of the Barons', into the charter.

The crisis grew out of John's failed wars to recover the lands in France he had lost to Philip II, ending in defeat at Bouvines in 1214. To pay for them John squeezed his barons with heavy feudal charges: records in the royal accounts show one baron paying 10,000 marks in inheritance tax in 1214 and another promising 20,000 marks for permission to marry. In May 1215 the rebels renounced their allegiance and took London, forcing John to negotiate.

The charter promised to protect the rights of the Church, to stop imprisonment without lawful judgement, to give swift justice and to limit the King's feudal payments, some of them only with the consent of the realm. Clause 61, the 'security clause', set up a council of 25 barons who could seize the King's castles and lands if he failed to put right a breach within 40 days; John ordered everyone to swear an oath to these 25.

The peace failed within weeks. Both sides had appealed to Pope Innocent III, John's overlord since 1213, and the Pope annulled the charter, which led to the First Barons' War. After John's death the regents of the young Henry III reissued a shortened charter in 1216 and again in 1217, when it first took the name Magna Carta; Henry III reissued it in 1225 in return for a tax, and Edward I confirmed it as statute in 1297.

Its fame came later. In the 17th century Sir Edward Coke used it against the claims of the Stuart kings, and the idea of ancient English liberties it came to stand for influenced the American colonists. Most historians now stress that in 1215 it dealt with the King and his barons rather than with the rights of ordinary people. Most of it has been repealed, but three clauses are still law in England and Wales.

Q160077.title: Fall of Constantinople
paras: On 29 May 1453 the army of the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II took Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire, after a siege that had begun on 6 April. The city was defended by Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos with Greek troops and Italian volunteers, among them the Genoese commander Giovanni Giustiniani, who led the defence of the land walls. Numbers are uncertain: modern estimates put the defenders at about 7,000-8,000 against an Ottoman army of perhaps 50,000-80,000.

By 1453 the empire had shrunk to little more than the city and a few outlying territories, its population thinned by plague and economic decline. The city had fallen only once before, to the Fourth Crusade in 1204. In 1452 Mehmed built the fortress of Rumeli Hisarı on the Bosphorus to control shipping to the city, and the West sent only small groups of volunteers; no large relief fleet arrived in time.

Ottoman bombards, including the great cannon cast by the engineer Orban, battered the ancient land walls, which the defenders repaired after each bombardment. A chain across the Golden Horn kept the Ottoman fleet out of the harbour until Mehmed had ships dragged overland on greased logs into the Horn. Ottoman mines under the walls were destroyed by Byzantine counter-mines. Constantine refused an offer to surrender. The final assault began after midnight on 29 May; when Giustiniani was badly wounded and carried away, the defence broke and the Ottomans entered the city.

Constantine XI died that day; how he died is not known for certain, and most accounts say he fell fighting in the streets. The city was sacked, and many inhabitants were killed or enslaved. Mehmed entered Hagia Sophia, which was turned into the city's chief mosque, and made Constantinople the Ottoman capital in place of Adrianople (Edirne).

The fall ended the Byzantine Empire, the last remnant of the Roman state. Many Greek scholars fled to Italy, taking Byzantine learning with them, and many historians use the year as a marker for the end of the Middle Ages.

Q6539.title: Storming of the Bastille
paras: On 14 July 1789 a crowd of armed Parisians, joined in the afternoon by mutinous soldiers of the French Guards, attacked and took the Bastille, a medieval fortress and state prison in eastern Paris. It was held by its governor, Bernard-René Jourdan de Launay, with about 82 invalides (veteran soldiers) and 32 Swiss grenadiers, while several thousand royal troops camped on the Champ de Mars did not intervene.

France was in financial crisis and the Estates-General, called in May 1789, had turned into a National Assembly in June. On 11 July Louis XVI dismissed his popular minister Jacques Necker, and Parisians feared that troops massing around the city would be used to crush the Assembly. On 13 July the electors of Paris formed a citizens' militia, and on the morning of the 14th a crowd seized tens of thousands of muskets at the Invalides but found no powder. Some 250 barrels of gunpowder had been moved to the Bastille, which is why the crowd went there.

Delegates from the city hall negotiated inside the fortress through the morning while the crowd grew. Around 1:30 p.m. attackers broke into the outer courtyard and cut the chains of a drawbridge, and shooting began. After 3 p.m. French Guards arrived with cannon. At about 5 p.m. de Launay stopped the firing and threatened to blow up the powder unless his men could leave; at about 5:30, short of food and water, he opened the gates. Around a hundred attackers and one defender were killed in the fighting; sources give slightly different totals.

De Launay was taken towards the Hôtel de Ville and killed by the crowd on the way, and the city's provost Jacques de Flesselles was also killed. Inside, the attackers freed only seven prisoners: four forgers, a man described as a lunatic, a man who had tried to kill Louis XV decades before, and a count held at his family's request.

The King recalled Necker, and on 17 July in Paris accepted the revolutionary cockade; Lafayette took command of the new National Guard. Nobles began to emigrate and the 'Great Fear' spread through the countryside. The Bastille was demolished within months, and 14 July became France's national day. Historians debate whether it was the Revolution's real starting point, but it became its great symbol.

Q1025466.title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
paras: On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BC, Gaius Julius Caesar was stabbed to death at a meeting of the Senate in the Curia of Pompey, part of Pompey's theatre complex in Rome. The ancient sources speak of about 60 conspirators, senators led by Marcus Junius Brutus, Gaius Cassius Longinus, Decimus Junius Brutus Albinus and Gaius Trebonius; Decimus posted gladiators nearby in the Portico of Pompey.

Caesar had won the civil war against Pompey and his allies and early in 44 BC was made dictator for life (dictator perpetuo). Many senators believed he meant to make himself king: Livy lists as last straws his failure to rise when a Senate delegation came to him, his removal of two tribunes after a diadem was placed on his statue, and the diadem Mark Antony offered him at the Lupercalia, which he refused. The conspirators called themselves defenders of the Republic.

As Caesar took his seat, Tillius Cimber came up as if to plead for his exiled brother and seized Caesar's toga; Caesar cried out that this was violence. One of the Casca brothers struck first, and the others joined in. Suetonius, writing about 160 years later, says Caesar received 23 wounds, and that the physician Antistius judged only the second, in the chest, to be fatal. Suetonius says he died without a word, only a groan, though some wrote that he said in Greek to Brutus, 'You too, my child?'; 'Et tu, Brute?' is Shakespeare's line. Three slaves carried the body home on a litter.

The killing did not restore the Republic. Mark Antony arranged a compromise under which the assassins went unpunished but Caesar's acts stayed valid. Caesar's will made his grandnephew Octavian his heir; in November 43 BC Octavian, Antony and Lepidus formed the Second Triumvirate, proscribed their enemies and defeated Brutus and Cassius at Philippi in 42 BC, the year Caesar was declared a god. Octavian, as Augustus from 27 BC, became the first Roman emperor.

Q221474.title: Columbus reaches the Americas (first voyage)
Q221474.place: The Bahamas, Cuba and Hispaniola (sailing for the Crown of Castile)
paras: Christopher Columbus, a Genoese navigator, sailed in the service of the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile. Under the Capitulations of Santa Fe, signed on 17 April 1492, they made him Admiral of the Ocean Sea and governor of any lands he found, with a share of their revenue. He planned to reach Asia by sailing west.

Three ships left Palos on 3 August 1492: the Santa María, owned by Juan de la Cosa and commanded by Columbus, the Pinta under Martín Alonso Pinzón and the Niña under Vicente Yáñez Pinzón, crewed largely by local volunteers recruited by Pinzón. After repairs and provisioning in the Canary Islands they left La Gomera on 6 September. Land was sighted in the night of 11 October and on 12 October they landed on an island its Taíno inhabitants called Guanahani, which Columbus named San Salvador; which modern island it was is disputed, though San Salvador Island in the Bahamas is the most likely. The seaman Rodrigo de Triana first sighted land, though Columbus later claimed the reward.

The fleet sailed on through the Bahamas, reached Cuba on 28 October and Hispaniola in early December, looking for gold; Columbus's own log tells of natives taken from San Salvador as guides. On 25 December the Santa María ran aground off Hispaniola and was wrecked; about 39 men were left at a fort called La Navidad, built from its timbers. The Niña and Pinta started home on 16 January 1493 and, after storms, a stop in the Azores and a call at Lisbon, reached Palos on 15 March 1493.

Columbus believed to the end that he had reached the edge of Asia. In 1493 the papal bull Inter caetera assigned the new lands to Castile, and in 1494 the Treaty of Tordesillas divided the non-European world between Spain and Portugal. The voyage began lasting European colonisation of the Americas and the exchange of plants and animals between the two hemispheres. Norse Greenlanders had reached Newfoundland about 500 years earlier, without lasting consequence.

Q179684.title: Spanish Armada
Q179684.place: The English Channel and the coast of Flanders
paras: In 1588 Philip II of Spain sent a great fleet, the Armada, to sweep the English Channel and escort the Duke of Parma's army from Flanders across to invade England. He meant to overthrow the Protestant Elizabeth I, end English support for the Dutch rebels and stop English privateers raiding Spanish ships and colonies. The execution of the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots, in February 1587 hardened his resolve, and Francis Drake's raid on Cádiz in April 1587 set the preparations back by about a year.

The fleet was commanded by the Duke of Medina Sidonia, a capable administrator with no experience at sea, appointed after the death of the admiral Santa Cruz. It left Lisbon with about 130 ships and close to 30,000 sailors and soldiers. The English fleet, under Lord Howard of Effingham with Drake and John Hawkins, had more ships but they were smaller and handier.

The Armada was sighted off the Lizard in Cornwall on 29 July (New Style). In a week of running fights off Plymouth, Portland and the Isle of Wight neither side did much damage, though the Spanish lost the flagship Nuestra Señora del Rosario, captured with its commander Pedro de Valdés. On 7 August the Armada anchored off Calais to wait for Parma, whose army was not ready. That night the English sent in eight fireships; none set a Spanish ship alight, but the Spanish cut their cables and scattered. The next day, 8 August, the English attacked the broken formation off Gravelines and sank or captured several ships.

A wind change saved the fleet from running onto the Flemish banks, but it could not return through the Channel and sailed home round Scotland and Ireland, where storms wrecked many ships. Estimates of the losses differ: Wikipedia gives about 44 ships lost and 11,000-20,000 dead, many from disease; other accounts say as many as half the fleet. Elizabeth's victory became a national legend, but the Anglo-Spanish War went on until 1604, and an English counter-armada in 1589 failed as badly.

cp05-01.title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
cp05-01.place: Wittenberg, Electorate of Saxony (Holy Roman Empire)
paras: On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor of theology at the University of Wittenberg in Electoral Saxony, sent a set of 95 Latin theses for academic debate to Albert, Archbishop of Mainz, under whose authority indulgences were being sold in the region.

The theses attacked the preaching and sale of indulgences, certificates said to reduce the punishment for sins after death. Johann Tetzel was selling them in a campaign whose proceeds went partly to rebuilding St Peter's Basilica in Rome. Luther argued that a truly repentant Christian already had full remission of penalty and guilt without indulgence letters, and that preachers who promised more misled the faithful.

The famous picture of Luther nailing the theses to the door of All Saints' Church in Wittenberg comes from a later account by his colleague Philip Melanchthon; Luther's own statements do not mention it, and historians debate whether it happened. What is certain is that the theses spread fast through print: several hundred Latin copies were printed in Germany in 1517, as pamphlets and placards in Basel, Leipzig and Nuremberg.

Theologians such as Johann Eck and Tetzel answered in print, and the Leipzig Debate of 1519 deepened the quarrel with Eck. The papal bull Exsurge Domine (1520) threatened him with excommunication; Luther burned it and was excommunicated in 1521. The theses are generally taken as the start of the Protestant Reformation, though Luther later said he was still a loyal 'papist' when he wrote them.

Q150995.title: Peace of Westphalia
Q150995.place: Münster and Osnabrück, Westphalia (Holy Roman Empire)
paras: The Peace of Westphalia is the name for the treaties signed at Osnabrück and Münster, the main ones concluded on 24 October 1648, that ended the Thirty Years' War in the Holy Roman Empire. The parties were the Emperor Ferdinand III, France, Sweden, their allies and the princes and cities of the Empire. Delegations had gathered in the two Westphalian towns from 1643 onwards.

A separate Peace of Münster between Spain and the Dutch Republic, signed on 30 January 1648, ended the Eighty Years' War and recognised Dutch independence. The Swiss Confederacy was recognised as legally independent of the Empire.

The settlement redrew the religious rules of the Empire: Calvinism was recognised alongside Catholicism and Lutheranism, 1 January 1624 became the 'normative date' that fixed which confession each territory kept, and subjects were no longer simply required to follow their ruler's faith. France received sovereignty over the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun and lands in Alsace; Sweden gained Western Pomerania, Wismar, the bishoprics of Bremen and Verden and an indemnity of five million thalers; Brandenburg gained Farther Pomerania; the Palatinate was divided with Bavaria.

Older histories treated the peace as the founding of a modern system of sovereign states. Most historians now call that the 'Westphalian myth': the treaty texts say nothing of the kind, and the Emperor lost less power than once claimed.

sources.title: Treaty of Westphalia: Peace Treaty between the Holy Roman Emperor and the King of France and their respective Allies

The Swiss Confederacy gained legal independence from the Empire.
France gained Metz, Toul and Verdun and Alsatian lands.
Sweden gained Western Pomerania, Wismar, Bremen and Verden and five million thalers; Brandenburg gained Farther Pomerania; the Palatinate was divided.
Calvinism was recognised; 1 January 1624 was the normative date; subjects no longer had to follow the ruler's religion.
Most historians call the sovereignty interpretation the 'Westphalian myth'.

Q48314.title: Battle of Waterloo
Q48314.place: Near Waterloo, south of Brussels (United Kingdom of the Netherlands; today Belgium)
paras: The Battle of Waterloo was fought on 18 June 1815 about 12 miles (20 km) south of Brussels, in what was then the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. Napoleon's French Army of the North, roughly 72,000-74,500 men, attacked an Anglo-allied army of about 68,000 under the Duke of Wellington, while a Prussian army of about 50,000 under Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher marched to join it. It was Napoleon's last battle.

Napoleon had taken power again in France in March 1815, beginning the 'Hundred Days'. Facing a Seventh Coalition, he struck first in the Low Countries, hoping to beat the British-led and Prussian armies separately before they could combine. On 16 June he defeated Blücher at Ligny while Wellington held Quatre Bras; he then sent about a third of his army, some 33,000 men, after the retreating Prussians, and that force was held up at Wavre and never reached Waterloo. Wellington drew up on a ridge near Mont-Saint-Jean.

Through the afternoon of 18 June Wellington's line withstood repeated French infantry and cavalry attacks. Around 6 p.m. Marshal Ney's troops took the farmhouse of La Haye Sainte in the allied centre, but Napoleon, distracted by the Prussians now attacking his eastern flank, did not reinforce him until after 7 p.m. By then Wellington had reorganised. Napoleon's last reserve, the Imperial Guard, attacked and was driven back; the allied army advanced along the whole line as the Prussians broke through on the French right, and the French army dissolved into rout.

Wellington's army lost about 17,000 men and Blücher's about 7,000; the French lost about 25,000 killed or wounded and some 8,000-9,000 captured. Napoleon abdicated four days later, and coalition troops entered Paris on 7 July. Waterloo ended the Hundred Days and the First French Empire; Napoleon spent his last years as a British prisoner on Saint Helena.
claims: The battle was fought on 18 June 1815 near Waterloo, about 12 miles south of Brussels.

Around 6 p.m. Ney took a farmhouse in the allied centre (La Haye Sainte); Napoleon did not reinforce him until after 7 p.m.

Q192050.title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
paras: On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, were shot dead in Sarajevo, capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which Austria-Hungary had annexed in 1908. The killer was Gavrilo Princip, a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb student.

Princip belonged to a group of young Bosnian conspirators linked to the Young Bosnia movement, which wanted to end Austro-Hungarian rule and unite the South Slavs. The Serbian secret society known as the Black Hand, whose leaders included the army officer Dragutin Dimitrijević ('Apis'), helped arm and train them, and the weapons were smuggled into Bosnia along a secret route. Each conspirator carried bombs or pistols and a cyanide capsule. Princip later said he also wanted to stop the reforms the Archduke planned, which might have strengthened the Slavic lands within the empire.

That morning, at about 10:15, one conspirator, Nedeljko Čabrinović, threw a bomb at the motorcade on its way to a reception at the city hall; it missed the Archduke's car and wounded about 16 to 20 people. After the reception the party set off again, the driver took a wrong turn, and as the car stopped nearby Princip stepped up and fired at close range. Both the Archduke and his wife died.

The killing set off the July Crisis: Austria-Hungary, blaming Serbia, declared war on it, and the alliance system turned that war into the First World War. Anti-Serb riots broke out in Sarajevo. Princip, too young at 19 for the death penalty, was sentenced to 20 years and died of tuberculosis in prison; older co-conspirators were hanged. In 1917 a Serbian court at Salonika tried Apis and other Black Hand leaders on charges now widely seen as fabricated, and executed them.

Q42976.title: October Revolution
paras: In the October Revolution the Bolshevik party, led by Vladimir Lenin, seized power in Petrograd from Russia's Provisional Government on 25-26 October 1917 by the Julian calendar then used in Russia, 7-8 November by the Gregorian. The rising was organised by the Military Revolutionary Committee of the Petrograd Soviet, which the Soviet had set up three weeks before the Congress of Soviets on a resolution of Leon Trotsky.

The February Revolution had brought down Tsar Nicholas II, but the Provisional Government, led by Alexander Kerensky, kept Russia in the unpopular world war amid food shortages and economic collapse. Workers and soldiers organised in soviets, and the Bolsheviks won support with anti-war slogans and the demand 'All power to the soviets'. After the July Days the party was repressed and Lenin went into hiding, but the failed Kornilov affair, a right-wing military move on Petrograd, led to the release of Bolsheviks including Trotsky and strengthened them. On 10 October (Old Style) the Bolshevik Central Committee voted for an armed rising.

On 24-25 October, after the government moved to close Bolshevik newspapers, Bolshevik forces under the Military Revolutionary Committee occupied the bridges, the telegraph office and other key points; the cruiser Aurora fired a signal shot. In the early hours of 26 October they entered the Winter Palace, where the government's ministers were, and arrested them, meeting little resistance; Kerensky had already left. The dramatic battle for the palace shown in later Soviet re-enactments and films largely did not happen.

The Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets, with a Bolshevik majority, approved the seizure of power; Mensheviks and right Socialist Revolutionaries walked out. It set up a Council of People's Commissars (Sovnarkom) headed by Lenin and adopted the Decree on Peace and the Decree on Land; further decrees nationalised banks and factories and brought in the eight-hour day. When elections to the Constituent Assembly gave the Bolsheviks only about a quarter of the seats, they dissolved it after its first sitting in January 1918. Civil war followed, ending in 1922 with the founding of the Soviet Union. Soviet historians presented the revolution as a popular uprising; many Western historians have called it a coup.
claims: The Bolsheviks under Lenin seized power in Petrograd on 25-26 October 1917 Old Style (7-8 November New Style).

Q488.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
paras: On 6 and 9 August 1945 the United States dropped atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. They were the product of the Manhattan Project. The Hiroshima bomb, 'Little Boy', was a uranium gun-type weapon dropped from the B-29 Enola Gay, commanded by Paul Tibbets; the Nagasaki bomb, 'Fat Man', was a plutonium implosion weapon, carried by the B-29 Bockscar under Charles Sweeney.

On 26 July the Allies' Potsdam Declaration demanded Japan's unconditional surrender and threatened 'prompt and utter destruction'; the Japanese government ignored it. Orders of 25 July listed Hiroshima, Kokura, Niigata and Nagasaki as targets.

Over Hiroshima on the morning of 6 August, Little Boy exploded about 1,900 feet above the city, close to where soldiers of the Japanese Second Army were exercising. President Truman announced the new weapon that day and warned of more if Japan did not surrender. On 9 August Bockscar's primary target was the arsenal city of Kokura, but it was hidden by smoke and haze; short of fuel, the crew turned to the secondary target, Nagasaki, where the bombardier dropped the bomb after glimpsing the city through the clouds.

Estimates of the dead by the end of 1945 range from 90,000 to 166,000 in Hiroshima and 60,000 to 80,000 in Nagasaki; an official US history estimates some 70,000 deaths in Hiroshima from the immediate effects of blast, heat and radiation. In the same days the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and invaded Manchuria. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August and signed the instrument of surrender on 2 September 1945. Whether the bombings were necessary to end the war, or were a war crime, is still debated.

Q43653.title: Apollo 11
Q43653.place: Launched from Kennedy Space Center, Florida (United States); landed in the Sea of Tranquility on the Moon
paras: Apollo 11 was the NASA mission that first landed people on the Moon. A Saturn V rocket launched it from Launch Complex 39A at the Kennedy Space Center on 16 July 1969 with Neil Armstrong as commander, Michael Collins as command module pilot and Edwin 'Buzz' Aldrin as lunar module pilot.

It answered the goal President John F. Kennedy set on 25 May 1961: to land a man on the Moon and return him safely to Earth before the end of the decade. The Soviet Union had led the early Space Race, launching the first satellite, Sputnik 1, in October 1957 and the first person in space, Yuri Gagarin, in April 1961.

On 20 July, Armstrong and Aldrin separated in the lunar module Eagle from the command module Columbia, which Collins kept in lunar orbit. Partly flown by hand by Armstrong, Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility at 20:17 UTC. About six hours later Armstrong stepped onto the surface, saying 'That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind'; Aldrin followed 19 minutes later. An estimated 650 million people watched on television. Their moonwalk lasted about two and a half hours, and they collected about 21.5 kg of lunar rock and soil.

After more than 21 hours on the surface, Eagle's ascent stage rejoined Columbia, and the crew splashed down in the Pacific on 24 July 1969, where USS Hornet picked them up. The landing fulfilled Kennedy's goal; a Soviet probe, Luna 15, crashed on the Moon on 21 July while Apollo 11 was there.

Q8707.title: Meiji Restoration
paras: The Meiji Restoration was the overthrow of the Tokugawa shogunate, the military government of the shōguns, and the return of practical power to the emperor. On 3 January 1868 Emperor Meiji declared political power restored to the Imperial House. The movement was led by the domains of Satsuma and Chōshū.

The shogunate was weakened by economic and political strains and by foreign pressure. In July 1853 the American Commodore Matthew Perry sailed four warships into Tokyo (Edo) Bay to force Japan to open regular trade with the West, which it had kept to a minimum for over two hundred years; the shogunate's acceptance of treaties on foreign terms, the 'unequal treaties', divided the samurai. Many rallied to the slogan sonnō jōi, 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians'.

Supporters of the Tokugawa fought on in the Boshin War of 1868-1869 and briefly in the Republic of Ezo, but by the early 1870s the emperor's government was unchallenged. Its aims were set out in the Charter Oath of 1868. In a few years it replaced the old currency, abolished the feudal domains and ended the privileged status of the samurai, and it set out to build industry and an army on Western models. Discontented samurai rose against these changes in the Saga Rebellion and the Satsuma Rebellion.

The Meiji Constitution of 1889 gave the new Empire of Japan its framework until the Allied occupation after the Second World War. Industrialised on Western lines, Japan went on to pursue colonial interests in East Asia. At the time it was called goishin, the 'honourable restoration'; it has also been translated as the Meiji Reformation.
